## Chapter 1

Politics, diplomacy, law, art, and history had opened no outlet for effort; winter in Portland Place was long, and Darwin was convulsing society. Lyell, Darwin’s geological champion and intimate of the Legation, promised introductions that never came; Adams read instead—the Origin, the Voyage. He became a Darwinist before the letter, a predestined follower of the tide, taking on trust the atomic theory, correlation of energy, kinetic gases, Natural Selection—the vast British habit of building systems on narrow foundations. Ignorant of mathematics, helpless to verify, he found it easier to assent than to contradict even such triflers as Tyndall and Huxley.

By rights he should have been a Marxist, but some New England trait blighted socialism; failing that, he turned Comteist within the limits of evolution—ready to be anything but quiet, eager for more upset, and then losing his hold by trying to understand. He never tried to understand Darwin; he fancied he could get the best of Darwinism from geology, a science idle minds could treat like history. Every curate in England dabbled in fossils; Adams cared for Evolution rather than for Selection, except as it might upset curates. Greedily he read Lyell’s Antiquity of Man (to wreck Eden) and then the new Principles, where Selection swelled to Evolution and at last to Uniformity. Unbroken Evolution under uniform conditions—this safe, conservative, Common-Law deity—suited a young man who had helped waste lives and treasure to enforce unity and uniformity; it had the charm of art. If Darwin, like a true Englishman, preferred to back into unity—to reach God a posteriori—any road was good that arrived.

Life depended on it. One had always been dragged between centralizations, and the proof that habit obeyed primordial law flattered self-esteem. One day, when Sir Charles came to have his Principles noticed in America, Adams rashly offered to do it if told what to say, and, after half an hour, sat down to clear American minds about their own profession. He meant to educate not them but himself; had Newton asked him to explain the Principia to Americans, he would have leapt, and would have begun by asking why the apple fell—what was Gravitation?—and been thrown off his base if told it was unknown.

At the outset he struck the Glacial Theory and thought it a chasm in uniformity. Lyell’s labored guesses seemed weak as hypotheses, worthless as proof. Adams ventured a sentence—Agassiz’s agent obliged Sir Charles to allow causes more violent than possible now—hoping for correction; Lyell let it stand. Doubt persisted; uniformity often worked queerly and not as Selection. Asked for a simplest case, Lyell gave Terebratula, identical from first to last—too much uniformity and too little selection. So Adams started at the end—himself—and begged the first vertebrate; to his bewilderment it was a very respectable fish, Pteraspis, reposing under his own loved Wenlock Edge.

By 1867 he knew Shropshire well: thirteenth-century Abbey, fifteenth-century Prior’s House, Roman road, ruins; time there lost sequence. Lying on the Edge, gazing across the Marches, one might mix epochs like Falstaff’s Shrewsbury clock without wrong. Best of all was to look south along the Edge toward Siluria, kingdom of the ganoid fish. Life began and ended there; behind lay Cambrian shells; beyond, crystalline rocks where all trace was erased.

Out of his Wenlock musings on Pteraspis Adams carried forward only the suspicion that evolution offered no proof of progress, and that the unity science promised was, like religion, a working hypothesis a historian should accept on faith or not at all.
